title: SUMIF and SUMIFS in Google Sheets: A Budgeting Guide
description: Learn SUMIF and SUMIFS in Google Sheets and Excel with seven budgeting examples, a free practice workbook and fixes for common mistakes.

cover.alt: A laptop showing a spreadsheet with highlighted green, yellow and blue cells next to an open notebook and a pen

keywords: sumifs google sheets sumif google sheets sumifs budget example sumifs date range sumif wildcard excel
takeaways: SUMIF adds up rows that match one condition. SUMIFS handles one or more, and its sum range comes first.
Seven examples cover categories, months, amounts over a limit, wildcards and "everything except".
Download the free practice workbook to try every formula on example spending data.
body:
If you learn one spreadsheet function for your money, make it `SUMIFS`. It answers the questions a budget is made of: how much did I spend on groceries? How much on eating out this month? How much went on the credit card? This guide explains `SUMIF` and `SUMIFS` in plain words, with seven examples on real-looking spending data. You can download the practice file and try every formula yourself.

Download the free SUMIFS practice workbook (.xlsx)

No sign-up needed. The formulas work the same way in Google Sheets and Excel. ![The Practice tab of the workbook, listing seven budgeting questions, the SUMIF or SUMIFS formula that answers each one, and the result](/assets/img/posts/sumifs-practice-preview-1260x510.webp) ## SUMIF: add up the rows that match one condition `SUMIF` looks down one column for rows that match a condition, and adds up the amounts in those rows. ``` =SUMIF(range, criterion, sum_range) ``` - **range** is the column to check, such as the categories - **criterion** is what to look for, such as `"Groceries"` - **sum_range** is the column to add up, such as the amounts In plain words: "look in the category column, find every row that says Groceries, and add up the amounts." ## SUMIFS: add up the rows that match several conditions `SUMIFS` does the same, but with as many conditions as you like. A row is only added if it matches **all** of them. ``` =SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criterion1, criteria_range2, criterion2, ...) ``` Notice the order changes. In `SUMIFS` the column to add comes **first**. In `SUMIF` it comes **last**. Mixing them up is the most common mistake with these functions, and Microsoft's own help page warns about it. Because `SUMIFS` works fine with just one condition too, many people use it for everything and never think about `SUMIF` again. ## The practice data The workbook's **Data** tab has 20 transactions from September and October 2026, in five columns: Date (A), Category (B), Description (C), Amount (D) and Paid with (E). The rows run from 5 to 24, so every range below is rows 5 to 24. The **Practice** tab shows each question, the formula and the result. A yellow "Your turn" column is there for you to type each formula yourself. ## Seven examples for your budget ### 1. Total spent on groceries ``` =SUMIF(Data!$B$5:$B$24, "Groceries", Data!$D$5:$D$24) ``` **Result: $362.30.** Every row whose category is Groceries, across both months. ### 2. Groceries in October only ``` =SUMIFS(Data!$D$5:$D$24, Data!$B$5:$B$24, "Groceries", Data!$A$5:$A$24, ">="&DATE(2026,10,1), Data!$A$5:$A$24, "<"&DATE(2026,11,1)) ``` **Result: $158.30.** Three conditions: the category is Groceries, the date is on or after October 1, and the date is before November 1. This is the formula behind every monthly budget, and it is exactly how our [expense tracker](/blog/track-expenses-google-sheets/) totals each month. The `&` joins the comparison sign to the date. Writing `">=2026-10-01"` as plain text can fail, depending on your spreadsheet's language settings, so building the date with `DATE` is the safe way. ### 3. Every purchase over $50 ``` =SUMIF(Data!$D$5:$D$24, ">50") ``` **Result: $1,387.60.** When you leave out the third part, `SUMIF` adds up the same column it checks. Useful for seeing how much of your spending comes from bigger purchases. ### 4. Eating out paid by card ``` =SUMIFS(Data!$D$5:$D$24, Data!$B$5:$B$24, "Eating out", Data!$E$5:$E$24, "Card") ``` **Result: $70.50.** Two conditions on two different columns. Note that "Card" only matches cells that say exactly "Card". Rows that say "Debit card" are not included. Text conditions match the whole cell, not part of it, unless you use a wildcard. ### 5. Anything with "coffee" in the description ``` =SUMIF(Data!$C$5:$C$24, "*coffee*", Data!$D$5:$D$24) ``` **Result: $21.50.** The asterisk `*` is a wildcard that means "any text". So `"*coffee*"` matches "Coffee", "Coffee and bagel" and "Coffee with a friend". Upper and lower case don't matter. This is a quick way to find out how much a habit costs. Try `"*uber*"` or `"*amazon*"` on your own data. ### 6. Everything except rent ``` =SUMIF(Data!$B$5:$B$24, "<>Rent", Data!$D$5:$D$24) ``` **Result: $754.30.** The `<>` sign means "not equal to". Rent takes a big, fixed share of a small income, so leaving it out shows you how much of your spending you can actually change. ### 7. A category typed in a cell ``` =SUMIF(Data!$B$5:$B$24, $B$3, Data!$D$5:$D$24) ``` **Result: $362.30** when cell B3 says Groceries. Instead of typing the category into the formula, you point to a cell. Change B3 to "Transport" and the answer changes to $130.00. This is how budget templates work: one formula, copied down a list of categories. ## Adding "this OR that" `SUMIFS` only does "and": every condition must match. For "or", add two formulas together: ``` =SUMIF(Data!$B$5:$B$24, "Groceries", Data!$D$5:$D$24) + SUMIF(Data!$B$5:$B$24, "Eating out", Data!$D$5:$D$24) ``` That gives $437.30: all food, whether bought at a shop or eaten out. ## Why your SUMIFS returns the wrong answer | Problem | What's going on | Fix | |---|---|---| | Result is 0 | The amounts are stored as text, often after pasting from a bank | Select the column and format it as a number, or retype one value to check | | A category is missing | A space or typo, such as "Groceries " with a space at the end | Use a dropdown for categories so the spelling is always the same | | Error message | The ranges are different sizes, such as D5:D24 and B5:B30 | Make every range cover the same rows | | Dates are ignored | The dates are text, not real dates | A real date can be formatted as a number. If it won't, retype it | | Wrong total after copying | The ranges moved when you copied the formula | Lock them with `$` signs, as in `$D$5:$D$24` | ## Where to go next The same pattern works for other functions you will meet in budgets: - `COUNTIFS` counts the matching rows instead of adding them, such as how many times you ate out this month. - `AVERAGEIFS` gives the average, such as your average grocery shop. - `MINIFS` and `MAXIFS` give the smallest or largest matching value. They need Google Sheets or Excel 2019 or newer. To see `SUMIFS` doing real work, open the [free monthly budget template](/blog/free-budget-template-google-sheets/). Its Actual column is one `SUMIFS` per category. ## Frequently asked questions **What is the difference between SUMIF and SUMIFS?** `SUMIF` takes one condition. `SUMIFS` takes one or more. The order of their parts is also different: the column to add goes last in `SUMIF` and first in `SUMIFS`. **Do these formulas work in Excel?** Yes. Both work the same way in Google Sheets and in Excel. **How many conditions can SUMIFS take?** Excel allows up to 127 pairs of range and condition. A budget rarely needs more than three. **Is SUMIFS case-sensitive?** No. "groceries" and "Groceries" match the same rows. **Can I match part of a word?** Yes, with wildcards. `*` stands for any text and `?` for a single character. To search for an actual asterisk or question mark, put a `~` in front of it. *This workbook is general information, not financial advice. The example numbers are made up to show the format.* ## Sources - [SUMIFS function, Google Docs Editors Help](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/3238496) - [SUMIFS function, Microsoft Support](https://support.microsoft.com/en-US/excel/functions/sumifs-function)
